I'm Devika, Wasim's cousin. I stayed with his family for the summer, so I can only say what I saw.
Wasim failed his Class 10 maths in May. His parents were fighting a lot then, doors banging. He spent most days in his room.
In June he started going to something he called 'the youth circle', in a rented hall near the bus depot. Two older boys came on a motorbike to pick him up. They brought him back late, with samosas for everyone, and called my aunt 'Aunty-ji' very politely.
Wasim smiled more. He started ironing his shirts. Once I heard him on the phone saying, 'They actually listen, yaar.'
When I asked what they did there, he said, 'Nothing, we just talk. They say I'm family now.'
Nobody had asked him for money or anything. I don't know what's going on in his head. But he'd never had that many phone calls before.

qa.a: It was in a rented hall near the bus depot.

qa.q: What might Wasim be feeling that makes the circle so appealing?
qa.a: He seems lonely and low after failing maths and hearing his parents fight, so being listened to and called family feels like a relief.

qa.a: They could spend real time with Wasim, ask openly and calmly about the circle, and talk to a trusted adult such as a school counsellor if anything worries them.

qa.a: Devika sees him happier and busier, but can't tell what is behind it, and the sudden warmth from older strangers makes Devika uneasy.

Since her father's shop in Sirsa closed, Ishita had stopped going to evening badminton. At home there was only silence and the ceiling fan, and her Class 11 marks had slipped.
Then Mona didi noticed her outside the new dance studio near the bus stand. "You look like someone carrying a heavy bag," she said, and let Ishita join for free. The girls there called each other sister. They remembered her name, asked about her exams, bought her lassi after practice. On Sundays they sat in a circle while Mona didi talked about "real discipline" and "finding your purpose when the world forgets you".
Ishita walked home those evenings feeling taller than she had in months. Nobody had asked her for anything. That was the strange, good part.
Her cousin Irfan noticed she now said "sister" in every sentence. "Who are these people?" he asked.
"Just friends," she said, and smiled as if she meant it.

qa.a: Sister.

qa.a: She felt seen and valued for the first time in months, after the loneliness and silence at home since the shop closed.

qa.q: What might a trusted adult do at this stage?
qa.a: Notice Ishita's loneliness, spend time with her, and ask gently about the group and its Sunday talks, without mocking it.

qa.q: What might Irfan be sensing when he asks 'Who are these people?'
qa.a: Irfan senses a sudden change in his cousin and feels curious and a little uneasy about a group he knows nothing about.

grounding: A lonely teen unsettled by family strain meets a warm group that offers attention, belonging and purpose before any demands.

Elif had been in Hamburg for four months, long enough to learn that nobody at school said her name right and that her parents stopped talking when she walked into the kitchen. The divorce papers sat on the fridge under a magnet.
Then Emil, the quiet boy from maths, said, "Come to the Circle on Friday. It's just people who get it."
The room above the bakery was warm and smelled of tea. Twelve people, mostly older teens and a few adults, sat on cushions. A woman named Marta said Elif's name perfectly on the first try. Everyone clapped when Elif said where she came from. They asked about her drawings and wanted to see them.
Marta said, "Here, you're never alone. The world outside doesn't understand people like us."
Walking home under the streetlights, Elif realised she hadn't felt this light since Izmir. She wished Friday would come again tomorrow.

qa.a: Above the bakery.

qa.a: The line that the outside world doesn't understand 'people like us'; talking with a parent or school counsellor about the group would help her see it clearly.
